entries.title: echo WebTransport streams after the client's address changes
entries.body:
Before this, a real-socket test carried stream data after a NAT rebinding only when the client's port changed. When its address changed, only datagrams were tested. The net_loopback WebTransport carrier now rebinds twice mid-session. First it moves to a new port on 127.0.0.1, then to 127.0.0.2. After each move it echoes eight rounds of a datagram and a new bidirectional stream. It then checks four things. The server validated the new path with a PATH_CHALLENGE. The server slot's whole 18-byte address, its address bytes and its port, equals the client's new address. The server's arena kept 0 bytes over the move. Nothing went to the old socket. The per-session 2 KiB arena band is unchanged. docs/wp34-network-stack.md now records #1210 as merged in #1218 and shipped in 0.35.0.

Fixes #1226
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: benchmark a consumer-only in-place ring mode
entries.body:
`bench/ring-inplace` gains a third mode, `consumer`. It splits the in-place path into its two halves: the producer renders into a private buffer and calls `tryPush`, as `copy` does, and the consumer lends the record with `peek`, `sendBody` and `release`, as `inplace` does. The consumer pops a record only when it has wrapped round the end of the ring, since `peek` cannot lend one.

The mode is now checked once in `main` and again in the producer, and an unknown mode exits non-zero. `run.mjs` reports bands and comparison rows for all three modes, and a new `--ring-bytes` option sets the ring size.

The bench also has these fixes:
- Every wait inside the run has a ten-second deadline. The drain and the reader had none.
- A response head that finds the previous tail still queued now drains and retries. Before, it failed the run.
- `body_bytes` prints to 2 decimals.
- A `stalls` counter records those retries. It read 0 in both quick runs, but stalls do happen in full runs, and how often there was not measured.

Which half of the in-place path is worth adopting:
- **The consumer half, at 10 KB.** It cuts consumer p50 by 14.8% with the 16 MiB ring and by 18.7% with the 1 MiB ring, with no measured pipeline difference. At 1 and 4 KB it makes no measured difference, apart from one 4 KB p99.
- **The producer half, at no size measured.** With the 16 MiB ring, in place is slower than copied over the pipeline at every size. Its cost is inferred from consumer against in place, which differ only in the producer half.

The cache explanation is undecided at 4 and 10 KB. The 1 MiB ring, small enough for one core's 2 MiB L2, brings the in-place gap inside its band, but no band covers a change across ring sizes. At 1 KB the explanation is not supported. No cache misses were counted.
metrics: consumer p50, consumer vs copied: +7.5% (±7.7%) / -3.2% (±9.0%) / -14.8% (±9.9%) at 1 / 4 / 10 KB with the 16 MiB ring, and +7.3% (±9.2%) / -7.3% (±13.5%) / -18.7% (±4.8%) with the 1 MiB ring. Pipeline, in place vs copied: +5.9% (±2.7%) / +3.8% (±2.5%) / +6.2% (±4.1%) at 16 MiB, and +7.8% (±5.3%) / +0.3% (±2.1%) / -0.8% (±2.0%) at 1 MiB. Pipeline, consumer vs in place at 16 MiB: -7.9% (±5.9%) / -2.8% (±1.9%) / -6.5% (±4.1%). 5 rounds x 2 runs x 50,000 messages per ring size. Intel Xeon @ 2.30 GHz, 4 CPUs, L2 2 MiB per core, L3 260 MiB. Consumer on CPU 0, producer on CPU 1, reader on CPU 2.

entries.title: mark regex internals private and document its API
entries.body:
`std/regex.ts` now shows only its API to the library reference. Of 220 class members, 169 that only their own class reads are `private`. 29 that another part of the module reads, such as the parser fields `Regex` compiles from and `Regex.build`, carry an `@internal` tag. The 22 public members are `Regex`'s `source`, `flags`, `groups`, `groupCount`, `groupIndex`, `test`, `exec`, `find`, `findAll`, `count`, `replace`, `replaceAll` and `split`, plus `RegexMatch`'s accessors.

Every public method, both constructors, `regexCompile` and `regexEscape` now say what each parameter and return value means: byte offsets, the -1 or "" a group that took no part gives, what `exec` leaves untouched on a miss, and the `regex: … at byte N` error. The six limit constants say that exceeding them is a compile error.

The compiler ignores visibility keywords, so no generated code changes. The one regenerated golden moves six `uncheckedGet` source positions, and its node ids and content are unchanged.

Part of #1236

entries.title: mark http client internals private and document its API
entries.body:
The HTTP client modules (`std/net/fetch.ts`, `http1-client-codec.ts`, `upstream.ts`, `outbound.ts`, `url.ts` and `websocket.ts`) now show only their API in the library reference. 92 members that only their own class uses are `private`. 55 that another part of the module or another std module reads, such as the response parser state the `http1Client*` helpers drive and the `WsDecoder` fields the websocket helpers read, carry an `@internal` tag. Members a guide page uses, such as `HttpBodyReader.client`, and limits users set, such as `UpstreamLimits.maxHeaderBytes`, stay public.

91 doc gaps are filled: constructors, methods, fields and the `WS_OP_*` and `WS_CLOSE_*` constants now say what each parameter and return value means. `Upstream.get` now says its path must be origin-form, starting with `/`. Otherwise the call ends with `UPSTREAM_E_REQUEST`, while `get` itself returns `UPSTREAM_E_NONE`.

Only comments and visibility keywords change. The compiler ignores visibility keywords, and no golden moved.

Part of #1236
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: mark http server internals private and document its API
entries.body:
The HTTP/1.1 server modules (`std/net/http1-server.ts`, `http1-codec.ts`, `http-fields.ts`, `http-compress.ts`, `handler.ts`, `router.ts`, `prefork.ts` and `buffer-pool.ts`) now show only their API in the library reference. 169 members that only their own class reads are `private`. Plumbing that another class or std module reaches into carries an `@internal` note naming the reader. Examples are the parser cursors `Http1Server` resets, the `Router` method spans `HttpHandler` reads, and the `BufferPool` fields the QUIC and HTTP/3 code uses. What the api-server guide shows users stays public: `HttpRequest.methodIs`, `pathIs`, `param`, `header` and the rest, and every `HandlerLimits` field, `jsonBytes` included.

About 150 functions and methods now say what each parameter and return value means. `HttpHandler`'s constructor says that `slots`, `jsonBytes`, `maxEvents` and `bodyTimeout` are read once, while `http` is kept by the carrier and read live. The `start` and `send` family name both causes of `HANDLER_DROPPED`: the connection closed, or the carrier's output is over half full. Three module-header examples are corrected to the real API: `http-compress` called a nonexistent `h2.write`, and `http1-codec` and `prefork` used names they did not import.

Only comments and visibility keywords change. The compiler ignores visibility keywords. Eight checked goldens move two `wrappingAdd` source positions each, with node ids and columns unchanged.

Part of #1236

entries.title: document the global builtins in nish.d.ts
entries.body:
Every global builtin in `runtime/nish.d.ts` now has a doc comment holding its whole reference: what it returns, its special cases and deviations from JavaScript, its errnos, its panic messages, its argument and position rules, the capability a call needs, and examples. An editor's hover and the generated library reference now say what `docs/LANGUAGE.md` → Builtins says. `Math`, the array and string receivers, `ReadonlyArray`, `Map` and `Set` gain merged interface declarations that carry their docs. They keep lib.es2022's exact signatures, so `tsc` accepts every program it accepted before.

The `nish/json-typed` exports document `jsonDecode`, `jsonEncode`, `JsonDecoder` and the error codes the same way, and their code is unchanged. `docs/LANGUAGE.md` stays the normative spec and loses no text. Each of its 12 builtin subsections links to the declarations.

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#builtins
Part of #1234

entries.title: link a wasm module for a page and load it without fetch
entries.body:
`scripts/build.sh --profile wasm-host` links a freestanding wasm module for a page to drive. It exports only the program's exported functions, `memory`, and the arena entry points the generated loader calls, where `--profile wasm` exports everything. `--memory <MiB>` fixes the initial and maximum memory at one size so the page's views never detach, and the stack is fixed at 64 KiB. `wasm-opt -Oz` runs when binaryen is on PATH, and the build line says whether it did. `--inline <file.mjs>` writes the module's bytes as `export const bytes = new Uint8Array([...])`. The other profiles refuse `--memory` and `--inline` with exit 2. `--profile wasm` is unchanged, byte for byte.

The `--emit-dts` loader now exports `load(source, imports)` and `loadSync(source, imports)`, and each takes bytes or a compiled `WebAssembly.Module`. The loader imports nothing and reads no URL, so a bundler can inline it as it stands. One-argument `load(bytes)` callers keep working. `nish/vite` is a Vite plugin: in `vite build` it compiles each configured entry, links it under `wasm-host --inline`, and answers the page's import of the entry with the module's exports, instantiated synchronously. Host imports and module storage are later WP50 stages.
metrics: add.wasm 316 -> 102 B raw (233 -> 111 gzip, 211 -> 87 brotli); arrays.wasm 2827 -> 2091 B raw (1479 -> 1092 gzip, 1302 -> 970 brotli); exact byte counts on linux-x64 without wasm-opt, guarded by the wasm-size block

entries.title: recommend one bcrypt batcher per process on several cores
entries.body: A single login batcher spanning every core cannot start a run while one is going, so at light load a login waits on the run in progress while other cores idle. A prefork server with one `cores: 1` batcher per worker overlaps the workers' runs instead. The bcrypt bench gains this as mode (d), and the security record, the password-hashing guide page and the bcrypt-batch module doc recommend it.
metrics: 4-vCPU Xeon, cost 10, 3 rounds, medians; p99 at 60 logins/s 123.1 ms against 139.4 ms for one batcher over all cores, burst throughput 246 against 223 logins/s; noise band 2% logins/s, 4% p50, 11% p99

entries.title: mark elliptic-curve crypto internals private and document their API
entries.body:
The elliptic-curve modules (`std/crypto/p256.ts`, `p384.ts`, `ed25519.ts`, `x25519.ts`) now show only their API in the library reference. The fields of every point and scratch class are read by the module's free functions, so they carry an `@internal` note rather than `private`. The same goes for the seventeen `f25519*` field helpers, which `nish/crypto/ed25519` imports. `P256SignScratch` stays exported, because `nish/net/tls` and the tests construct it, and its fields are `@internal`.

Every exported function now says what its parameters and results mean. `ed25519` and `x25519` gain header examples, and the `p256` and `p384` examples are replaced with ones that compile as written (the old ones called an undefined `readKey` and used an unimported `sha256`). The `x25519` doc no longer says nothing in the tree refuses an all-zero shared secret: `nish/net/tls` refuses it on both sides of the handshake, and any other caller must still check it. No stated wipe, constant-time, clamping or point-validation property changes.

Only comments change: the comment-free syntax tree of all four files is identical to the base, and no golden moved.

Part of #1236

entries.title: mark symmetric crypto and hash internals private and document their API
entries.body:
The symmetric crypto and hash modules (`std/crypto/aes.ts`, `chacha20poly1305.ts`, `hmac.ts`, `hkdf.ts`, `sha1.ts`, `sha256.ts`, `sha512.ts`, `bcrypt.ts`, `bcrypt-batch.ts`, `base64url.ts`, `ct.ts`) now show only their API in the library reference. Members only their own class reads are `private`, such as the HMAC scratch pads and the `BcryptBatcher` queue. The hash state `nish/crypto/hmac`, `nish/net/postgres` and `nish/crypto/ed25519` reach into carries an `@internal` note naming the reader. The `AesKey` fields and the SHA `state`, `block` and `schedule` arrays stay public because tests build or read them.

Every export and public method now says what its parameters and results mean, with each security contract stated on the function it governs: nonce and IV reuse, key lengths, `null` on a failed tag with no plaintext produced, and what the caller still wipes. Two docs are corrected against the code:
- `BcryptBatcher.run` does not answer in arrival order: bad-salt answers come first, then verifies grouped by cost, then hashes, so callers match answers by `ticket`;
- `hkdfExpandInto` panics, before writing anything, on a hash length other than 32 or 48 or an output window outside `out`.

Only comments and visibility keywords change: the comment-free syntax tree of all eleven files is identical to the base, and no golden moved.

Part of #1236

entries.title: document the nish: modules in JSDoc on nish.d.ts
entries.body:
Each `declare module "nish:*"` block in runtime/nish.d.ts now carries its module's reference documentation, so the pages `node scripts/gen-reference.mjs` generates under docs/reference/ carry it as well. The blocks are fs, process, net, unsafe, simd, io, term, secret, region and async. Each module comment has a one-sentence lead, an indented usage example, then paragraphs. Each export has a description, plus `@param` and `@returns` where they apply. Signatures are unchanged.

docs/LANGUAGE.md remains the normative spec. Its Builtins subsections keep the type rules, refusals and diagnostics, panics, platform differences, and ownership and security rules. What each function takes and returns, the examples and the per-function notes moved to the JSDoc, and each subsection now links its reference page. Headings and anchors are unchanged. Every fact removed from the spec appears in the JSDoc.

The nish-secret and nish-region pages are generated from std/secret.ts and std/region.ts, so the JSDoc on those two module blocks shows in editors but not on those pages.

entries.title: import a wasm module's host functions from the page's TypeScript
entries.body:
A Nish module built for a page can import the functions the page supplies
straight from the page's own TypeScript. The compiler reads a host module,
named by `--host <file>` or by `"nish": { "host": [...] }` in the root
package.json, for its exported signatures and skips each body unparsed. Each
imported function becomes a wasm import from module `host`
(`"wasm-import-module"="host"`), costed and pessimised like a C call and
carrying the `ffi` capability. The generated loader passes an
`i32`/`f32`/`f64`-only function straight through and wraps the rest once, at
load. `--emit-dts` types what the page owes as `Imports`, `--emit-ts` keeps
the import line, and `nish/vite` passes the host modules itself.

A host object crosses as `HostHandle<"kind">`, a nominal `i32` that only an
import makes. It compares only with its own kind and `0`, and has no
arithmetic or number conversion. tsc reads the same type,
`(number & { readonly __nishHostKind: K }) | 0`, so both checkers refuse a
wrong kind or a forged number.

Every crossing that would copy or allocate in secret is refused, and each
refusal names the explicit form. That covers a string result; an object,
class, function, Promise, `unknown` or `any`; and, until stages 4 and 3, a
string or typed-array parameter. A `declare function` is now refused in a
build that makes a page module (`--target wasm32`, or `--emit-dts` on a
native target), because wasm-ld would let a C definition replace an import.
It stays legal natively and under WASI. A host module is refused in a native
or WASI build.

Measured: an import entry is 7 B plus its name, about 20 B for a name like
  `hCanvas`; the stage-1 wasm-size rows are unchanged, and a program with no
  host module is byte-identical (of 1449 checked goldens only the six emit-ts
  modules of src/ moved, for Walk's new field)

entries.title: close the std API-visibility acceptance gaps
entries.body:
The last gaps in std's public documentation are closed.

Every exported function in `std/net/url.ts`, `websocket.ts`, `outbound.ts`, `fetch.ts` and `http1-client-codec.ts` now has an `@param` per parameter and an `@returns`. Each gives the function's sentinels, refusals and panics. Nineteen public constructors in the DNS, TLS, QUIC and P-256 modules gain a description, and four `QuicConnection` fields gain one too.

The library reference no longer shows the `Regex` constructor, which only `regexCompile` calls, or the two `QuicStreams` counters that only their own class reads.

Two docs are stated against the code:
- **P-256 signing:** the `P256SignScratch` and `TlsP256Signer` scratch makes the base-point multiplication work in reused arrays, and a signature keeps nothing after the call. It does not make signing allocation-free.
- **HTTP/1 request heads:** the `names` must hold exactly one `Host`, the caller's own field, which is written first.

Only comments and visibility keywords change: the comment-free syntax tree of every touched file is identical to the base. Two goldens move by position only, and the reference pages are regenerated.

Part of #1236
